children: Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok has flagged a costly fiscal decision: the U.S. Treasury did not lock in longer maturities when rates sat near zero.
Corporations, by contrast, refinanced aggressively at record-low fixed coupons during the pandemic. Corporate net interest expense has since fallen to 0.4% of GDP.

The federal government left the maturity profile of its outstanding debt largely unchanged and now pays net interest equal to 3.6% of GDP. Because the rise in rates landed almost entirely on the public balance sheet rather than on private firms, the tightening cycle that began in 2022 failed to deliver the usual slowdown in activity.

That corporate cushion is temporary. Pandemic-era borrowings are rolling over into higher coupons, and the drag will be sharpest for highly leveraged borrowers in credit markets—software issuers among them.

Slok’s conclusion is that the monetary-policy transmission mechanism was delayed, not disabled. It still operates through the familiar channel: the more debt a borrower carries, the greater the damage from elevated rates. High-quality companies with modest leverage and genuine earnings, therefore, look more attractive on both the debt and equity sides of the market.

title: Firms locked in cheap debt, Washington didn’t and the bill is now 3.6% of GDP
